title: Anxious about the winner, calm about the count

pages.title: Seven in ten are stressed by the vote; eight in ten trust the count
Seven in ten are stressed by the vote; eight in ten trust the count, continued

seven-in-ten-are-stressed-by-the-vote-ei.title: Seven in ten are stressed by the vote; eight in ten trust the count
seven-in-ten-are-stressed-by-the-vote-ei.dek: On the eve of the US midterms, the anxiety is about the result. The machinery that produces it is trusted more than the mood suggests.
seven-in-ten-are-stressed-by-the-vote-ei.text: Tomorrow Americans vote in the midterm elections, and the feeling in the room is not hard to read. In a survey of 1,000 US adults conducted online by Dynata for LifeStance Health in October, 70% said they felt at least some stress or anxiety about the vote on 3 November, and 43% reported a moderate or significant amount [1]. That is the number that will be quoted this week. It is worth reading next to a second one. The mood. The stress is not evenly spread. More than half of Gen Z respondents (55%) and 48% of millennials reported moderate or significant stress [1]. Among full-time employees the figure was 51%, and 47% said they would probably or definitely take a mental health day after election day if they could [1]. Asked about the political climate in general, 42% said they felt anxious about the future and a quarter (25%) reported hopelessness or a sense of “doom” [1]. Some of the coping is new. About one in four respondents (26%) said they had used an AI chatbot to talk through political or election stress, rising to 41% of Gen Z and 6% of baby boomers [1]. Fewer than one in three (32%) had a plan to protect their mental health on election night; another 27% said they had none but thought they should [1]. And the dread has a long tail: 37% said they were already dreading political conversations at family gatherings over the holidays, and 31% would rather wash all the dishes [1]. A caution before going further. This is a company survey, by a mental health provider, with a stated interest in the subject [1]. Its numbers describe feelings honestly reported, not diagnoses. They are a thermometer, not a chart from a clinic. The machinery. Now the second number. Pew Research Center surveyed 5,062 US adults, including 3,917 registered voters, from 28 September to 4 October [2]. It found that American voters “generally expect” the midterms to be run and administered well, and that this view is shared by similar majorities on both sides [2]. Nearly eight in ten voters (79%) were at least somewhat confident that votes cast in person would be counted as voters intend; among those backing Republican candidates it was 84%, among those backing Democrats 81% [2]. The trust is not unconditional, and Pew is careful to say where it thins. Confidence that mail and absentee ballots will be counted as intended was 53% overall [2]. Among Democratic voters it was 64%, down from 88% in the 2022 midterms; among Republican voters it was 42%, modestly higher than before [2]. Roughly half of voters (52%) were confident the systems are free from hacking [2]. And the two sides worry about different things: 19% of Republican voters mentioned fraudulent or illegitimate votes, while Democratic voters were more likely to raise legitimate voters being denied access (10%) or interference in election administration by the Trump administration (11%) [2]. Pew notes its survey was taken before the Justice Department sued California on 15 October over mailed ballots [2]. Still, the core holds. Two-thirds of voters were confident that people who try to intimidate voters at polling places will be stopped [2]. Seven in ten Democratic voters (70%) and 61% of Republican voters expected Americans to know who won within a day or two of election day [2]. What the two numbers say together. Desk arithmetic: the share of adults stressed about the vote (70%) [1] and the share of voters confident in the in-person count (79%) [2] cannot both describe separate minorities. They come from different surveys and different samples, so they cannot be added or netted. But taken side by side, they imply that a great many Americans hold both views at once: anxious about who wins, and fairly calm about whether the win will be counted properly. That is a healthier combination than the headlines suggest. Anxiety about outcomes is what people feel when an election matters. Distrust of the count is what they feel when the institution has failed. The surveys show plenty of the first and, for the in-person ballot at least, a minority of the second. The weak spots are specific and named: postal ballots, hacking, and a partisan split over who might be wrongly let in or kept out [2]. Specific worries can be answered by specific procedures, and that is the dull work of county clerks, poll workers and canvassing boards this week. For you. If you follow the count from Europe tomorrow night, the useful habit is the one the clerks use: wait for the official tally, and separate how you feel about the result from what you know about the process. Your stress about the winner is your own business. Your confidence in the counting can rest on evidence, and the evidence, read carefully, is steadier than the mood.

podium-vs-print-a-complex-international.title: Podium vs Print: "a complex international environment" and 48.7
podium-vs-print-a-complex-international.dek: Beijing's statistician explained October's factory slip with the calendar and the world outside. The export-order line put a number on the second half of that sentence.
podium-vs-print-a-complex-international.text: The podium. On Saturday China’s National Bureau of Statistics reported that its official manufacturing purchasing managers’ index fell 0.8 points to 49.3 in October [1]. Huo Lihui, a chief statistician with the bureau, gave two reasons, Xinhua reported: some demand had been brought forward ahead of the National Day holiday, and “a complex international environment” [1]. The rest of the official reading leaned on the bright side: high-tech manufacturing at 51.3, equipment at 50.6, and railway, shipbuilding, aerospace and electronics above 53 on both production and new orders [1]. The print. The sub-index that measures the “international environment” most directly is new export orders. It fell to 48.7 from 50.0 in September [2]. The headline reading also missed the 50.0 that economists polled by Reuters had expected, and the non-manufacturing index slipped to 49.7, with construction at 48.0 [2]. Below 50 means more purchasing managers reported falling orders than rising ones. The gap. The statistician and the index do not contradict each other; the index simply sizes the phrase. Desk arithmetic: export orders fell 1.3 points, more than the headline’s 0.8. A holiday that pulls demand forward should show up at home as much as abroad, yet total new orders fell 1.1 points to 49.4 [1]. And the pain is not shared evenly: large firms stayed at 50.2, medium-sized firms read 48.4 and small firms 47.5 [2]. The shipbuilders, aerospace and electronics makers are still expanding; the small workshop is where “complex” lands. What the speech left out. Prices. The purchasing-price index fell 4 points to 56.8 and factory-gate prices eased 2.3 points to 51.7 [1]. For you, buying from China, that is the useful line: input costs are still rising, but more slowly, and a supplier with thin export orders has more reason to talk. Read the sub-indices before the commentary. Nothing here is investment advice.

eight-ships-no-tankers-hormuz-on-a-sunda.title: Eight ships, no tankers: Hormuz on a Sunday
eight-ships-no-tankers-hormuz-on-a-sunda.dek: One counter's tally for 1 November is small enough to read ship by ship. That is the news.
eight-ships-no-tankers-hormuz-on-a-sunda.text: On Sunday, 1 November, eight AIS-visible commercial ships crossed the Strait of Hormuz, according to the hormuz.now counter: five inbound into the Gulf, three outbound to the Gulf of Oman [1]. None of them was a tanker; all eight were bulk carriers or general cargo ships [1]. One of them, the bulk carrier Forever Happy, crossed twice, outbound at 02:17 CET and back inbound at 05:54 CET, both bound for Sharjah [1]. The counter puts its seven-day average at 9.0 crossings a day, against a pre-crisis baseline of 84.8 [1]. Desk arithmetic: that is about 11% of normal traffic, and Sunday’s eight is a little below even that. The declared destinations are short hops (Sharjah, Sohar, Al Suwaiq, Kandla), the trade of a neighbourhood rather than an ocean [1]. Two cautions belong next to any single count. First, it measures only ships with their transponders on and above the counter’s commercial threshold; it logged eight further small-craft crossings it left out [1]. Second, the slower, official cross-check, IMF PortWatch, has not published this day yet; its latest figure is for 25 October [1]. For you, the useful part is the zero. Oil prices are quoted by the minute; the tankers that would ease them are counted one by one, and on Sunday the count for them was nil. Nothing here is investment advice.

eight-days-to-10-november-and-the-notice.title: Eight days to 10 November, and the notices still say November
eight-days-to-10-november-and-the-notice.dek: Both governments said the US–China truce would run to January. The documents at the border have not caught up.
eight-days-to-10-november-and-the-notice.text: In September both Washington and Beijing said their trade truce, due to lapse on 10 November, would be extended to 10 January 2027 [1]. As of 1 November, a tracker of the legal texts finds only one formal step: a US Trade Representative proposal to keep the maritime port-fee action suspended to 9 January, with comments closed on 30 October and no final notice yet [1]. China’s own suspension notice still reads 10 November [1]. What hangs on the old dates: 178 US Section 301 exclusions expiring at 11:59 p.m. EDT on 9 November (04:59 CET on 10 November), and China’s October 2025 export-control package on rare earths and battery materials [1]. For you, if you import, the advice is old and dull: price your November entries on the law as published, not as announced. Speeches move markets; notices move customs.

35-basis-points-off-the-ten-year-in-octo.title: 35 basis points off the ten-year in October, and a week that sets the receipt
35-basis-points-off-the-ten-year-in-octo.dek: October's bond rally ran from two years to thirty. This week, payrolls, a factory survey and Apple's quarter get to check the arithmetic.
35-basis-points-off-the-ten-year-in-octo.text: October was the month the bond market gave something back. On the US Treasury’s own daily table, the 10-year par yield closed September at 5.29% and October at 4.94% [1]. Desk arithmetic: that is 35 basis points lower in a month. The 2-year fell from 4.88% to 4.56%, the 5-year from 5.09% to 4.71%, and the 30-year from 5.64% to 5.31% [1]. The one that barely moved. The 3-month bill went from 4.20% to 4.16% [1]. Desk arithmetic: 4 basis points, against 32 to 38 for everything from two years out. Bills track the policy rate the Fed has already set; longer bonds price what people expect next. October changed the expectation, not the rate. Where it stands this morning. Reuters had the 10-year at 4.952% in Asian trading, well below its October peak of 5.3645%, with the 2-year at 4.612% [2]. Fed funds futures still imply a 72% chance of a quarter-point rise in December, Reuters reported, but only 55 basis points of total tightening is now priced, against more than 70 a month ago [2]. The Nasdaq lost almost 7% in October, its worst month since April 2025 [2]; the bond market’s gain was partly the stock market’s loss. The week’s receipts. The ISM factory survey lands later on Monday, and the payrolls report on Friday, where the median forecast is for 65,000 new jobs after September’s 29,000, with unemployment holding at 4.2% [2]. Apple holds its results call at 2:00 p.m. Pacific on Monday [3]; with US clocks back on winter time since Sunday, that is 23:00 in Berlin. The calm point. You do not need to guess the week. Each of these numbers arrives on a fixed date, from an institution with a publication calendar, and each will be revised in public. Let the invoices speak in order. Nothing here is investment advice.

kioxia-down-15-tsmc-up-2-asia-sorted-its.title: Kioxia down 15%, TSMC up 2%: Asia sorted its chips one by one
kioxia-down-15-tsmc-up-2-asia-sorted-its.dek: After Friday's Nasdaq slide, Monday's Asian session did not sell 'tech'. It sold some companies and bought others, which is how it should work.
kioxia-down-15-tsmc-up-2-asia-sorted-its.text: The headline said “mixed”. The detail said “selective”. Japanese chipmaker Kioxia fell more than 15% after a cautious outlook that missed forecasts, AFP reported via CNA, and is now down around 70% from its June record while still up more than 200% this year [1]. Samsung fell more than 1%; SK hynix rose more than 1%; TSMC added nearly 2% [1]. By midday Tokyo, Sydney, Singapore and Taipei were down, while Seoul, Hong Kong and Shanghai were up [1]. Earlier in the session Reuters had the Nikkei 0.5% lower and South Korea 0.8% lower, after Korean shares shed 16% in October [2]. Morning trade turns quickly; the closing prints are the ones to keep. The worry has a number. Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft and Meta are on track to spend more than $700 billion on capital investment this year, according to analyst estimates cited by CNA [1]. Goldman Sachs analysts put hyperscaler capex near $800 billion this year and $1.2 trillion in 2027, Reuters reported [2]. “Earnings growth is strong, but it is no longer accelerating,” wrote Goldman’s Ben Snider [2]. The quieter number. Bloomberg counted 90% of S&P 500 software companies beating profit expectations this season but only 70% topping revenue, CNA reported [1]. Profits are an estimate; sales are invoices. When the two drift apart, the invoices are the ones worth reading. Nothing here is investment advice.

52-0-and-49-3-chinas-two-factory-surveys.title: 52.0 and 49.3: China's two factory surveys disagree
52-0-and-49-3-chinas-two-factory-surveys.dek: The private gauge stayed in growth for an 11th month. The official one slipped back below 50. Both are right about different factories.
52-0-and-49-3-chinas-two-factory-surveys.text: The RatingDog China manufacturing PMI read 52.0 for October, just under September’s 52.1 and in line with forecasts, Investing.com reported. It is the 11th month in a row above the 50 line [1]. Output grew at its fastest pace since April [1]. The official NBS index fell to 49.3 from 50.1, missing forecasts of 49.9 [1]. The two surveys cover different firms. The official one leans towards large and state-owned manufacturers; RatingDog has more small and private ones [1]. One detail matters more than either headline. Input costs rose for a 16th month, but selling prices fell for the second time in three months as competition pushed firms to discount [1]. Final October factory readings from India, Australia, the UK and the US are due later on Monday, NDTV Profit noted [2]. Nothing here is investment advice.

54-8-million-ballots-in-and-none-of-them.title: 54.8 million ballots in, and none of them counted yet
54-8-million-ballots-in-and-none-of-them.dek: On the eve of the US midterms, the number to watch is not a poll. It is the hour at which each state is allowed to open an envelope.
54-8-million-ballots-in-and-none-of-them.text: By late Sunday, US Eastern time, 54,834,584 Americans had already voted in Tuesday’s midterms, by NBC News’s count: about 24 million by mail and 30.8 million in person [1]. A further 60.7 million mail ballots had been requested or sent, a figure that includes every registered voter in states that post a ballot to everyone [1]. Desk arithmetic: in-person early votes are about 56% of the total so far. Not one of these ballots has been counted in the sense that matters to you. As the University of Florida’s Election Lab reminds readers of its tracker, party-registration statistics “are not actual votes” [4]. And no state allows results to be released until its polls close on Election Day, the Center for Election Innovation & Research notes [2]. What differs is the preparation. At least 45 states and Washington, DC, allow or require envelope processing (checking signatures and IDs, sorting) before Election Day; at least 33 allow ballots to be scanned into tabulators early, without producing totals [2]. Only three, Alaska, Alabama and Mississippi, do not permit scanning until polls close [2]. Pennsylvania is the slow lane by law, not by fault. Its counties may not open a mail ballot until 7 a.m. on Election Day, on the same day they run more than 9,000 polling places, and may not publish mail-ballot results until polls close at 8 p.m. [3]. Ballots must arrive by 8 p.m.; a postmark does not help, except for some military and overseas voters [3]. Wisconsin is similar: envelopes cannot be formally processed until the polls open [2]. So expect the familiar shape: early totals that move as mail ballots are added, in different orders in different states. That movement is the machinery doing its job, not a sign of anything amiss; Pennsylvania’s own officials say changes after election night “are not evidence” of rigging [3]. Media calls are projections on unofficial results [3]. For you, the useful habit is to ask of each state not “who is ahead?” but “what has been counted?”

serbias-last-53-polling-stations-and-a-c.title: Serbia's last 53 polling stations, and a count that closed
serbias-last-53-polling-stations-and-a-c.dek: A week after the vote, Serbia reran the ballot where results could not be established. The totals barely moved; the procedure is the point.
serbias-last-53-polling-stations-and-a-c.text: On Sunday Serbia’s Republic Electoral Commission published results from all 8,392 polling stations in the snap parliamentary election of 25 October, after voting was repeated at 53 of them [1]. The Student List won 53.01% of the vote; “Aleksandar Vučić – United Serbia” won 38.98% [1]. Ivica Dačić’s list took 2.13% [1]. Turnout was 4,444,310 voters, or 68.89% of the register [1]. The rerun was small and specific. At 31 polling stations local commissions had ruled that the result could not be established; at 22 the vote had been annulled [1]. In all, 24,438 citizens were entitled to vote again, from 07:00 to 20:00 [1]. At one station in Zemun the reason was plain arithmetic: the number of voters who signed the register did not match the number of ballots, Tanjug reported [1]. Desk arithmetic: the preliminary count, from 8,338 stations, had the Student List on 53.04% and the Vučić list on 38.97% [1]. A week of complaints, annulments and reruns moved each by three hundredths of a point or one hundredth. That is what a working count looks like: disputes settled station by station, in public, by the commissions the law names, before anyone sits in parliament. The seat allocation follows from these totals; the commission’s own seat figures are the ones to wait for.

bulgaria-counted-half-its-protocols-by-m.title: Bulgaria counted half its protocols by midnight
bulgaria-counted-half-its-protocols-by-m.dek: A presidential runoff, a preliminary count, and a column for voters who backed nobody.
bulgaria-counted-half-its-protocols-by-m.text: Bulgaria held the second round of its presidential and vice-presidential election on Sunday. By midnight, Sofia time, the Central Election Commission had begun publishing preliminary results, with 52.42% of polling-station protocols processed by the district commissions [1]. On that count, Iliana Iotova and her running mate Kiril Valchev had 57.95%; Andrey Gyurov and Georgi Kandev had 39.01% [1]. The third line is the one other countries lack: “I do not support any candidate”, at 3.04% [1]. It is a small, formal way to turn up and say no, and it is counted like everything else. These are preliminary figures on just over half the protocols, not a result. For you, the habit is the same as in America this week: read the share counted before the share won.

the-painter-and-the-inventor-are-not-the.title: The painter and the inventor are not the same patient
the-painter-and-the-inventor-are-not-the.dek: A study of 14,658 Swedish twins finds artistic creativity goes with somewhat poorer mental health, and scientific creativity mostly does not.
the-painter-and-the-inventor-are-not-the.text: The idea that genius and “madness” go together is old; the evidence for it, says Miriam Mosing, co-senior author of a new paper in Molecular Psychiatry, “remains mixed” [1]. Researchers at the Max Planck Institute for Empirical Aesthetics, Karolinska Institutet and other institutions tried to sort it out with twins [1]. The data. They used two Swedish surveys, from 2012–2013 and 2022–2023, covering 14,658 twins, 6,419 of whom answered both [1]. The surveys measured achievement in music, writing, dance, theatre and visual arts, and separately in science and invention; mental health came from self-reported symptoms and from psychiatric diagnoses in Swedish medical records [1]. Comparing identical twins, who share almost all genes and their upbringing, lets researchers strip out much of what families have in common [1]. The finding. Higher artistic creativity went with “somewhat more mental health problems”, and genes played an important role in that link, says first author Penghao Xia [1]. Scientific creativity was not significantly linked to most conditions; some measures even went with fewer difficulties [1]. Earlier depressive symptoms predicted greater openness to experience later, even between identical twins, a hint of a causal path that the authors say still needs confirming [1]. Why it matters. The lesson is about measurement: lump all creativity together and the differences cancel out, which may be why earlier studies disagreed [1]. For you, the practical reading is modest. A creative child is not a worry in waiting, and a lab bench is not a cure. The authors stress that environment still matters [1].

a-bow-adds-15-points-in-japan-and-almost.title: A bow adds 15 points in Japan and almost none in America
a-bow-adds-15-points-in-japan-and-almost.dek: A courteous gesture made faces look more attractive to Japanese raters and left Americans unmoved. Manners, not instinct.
a-bow-adds-15-points-in-japan-and-almost.text: Researchers led by Takayuki Osugi of Yamagata University showed computer-generated faces of four racial appearances either standing still or bowing, and asked people to rate attractiveness from 0 to 100 [1]. Japanese raters scored bowing faces roughly 6 to 12 points higher for a short bow and 15 to 28 points higher for a long one, whatever the face’s appearance [1]. For female European models, the scores went from 43.2 static to 59.0 with a long bow [1]. American raters, recruited online, barely moved: gaps were typically under three points, and for the same models the averages were 56.5, 57.4 and 56.9 [1]. They could still tell attractive faces from less attractive ones, so they were paying attention [1]. The samples were small, 30 to 49 people per sub-experiment, and the faces were avatars on home screens [1]. The point survives: politeness is learned, and what we learn shapes what we see.

259-31-for-monday-after-a-weekend-that-u.title: €259.31 for Monday, after a weekend that used less power and paid nearly as much
259-31-for-monday-after-a-weekend-that-u.dek: Germany drew about a sixth less electricity on Sunday than on Friday. The price fell by less than a twentieth. The missing ingredient was wind.
259-31-for-monday-after-a-weekend-that-u.text: Monday’s power was priced on Sunday, and it is not cheap. The day-ahead auction set an average of €259.31 per megawatt hour for Germany and Luxembourg on Monday 2 November, according to the Bundesnetzagentur’s SMARD figures [1]. That follows €251.42 on Saturday and €255.91 on Sunday [1]. The weekend that didn’t discount. Grid load fell, as it does when factories and offices close: 1,349.8 gigawatt hours on Friday, 1,168.2 on Saturday and 1,112.5 on Sunday [1]. Desk arithmetic: Sunday used about 17.6% less electricity than Friday, while its price was about 4.7% lower than Friday’s €268.62 [1]. Less demand, almost the same bill. The reason is in the air. Onshore wind turbines generated 688.8 gigawatt hours on Monday 26 October; this Sunday, 79.0 [1]. Offshore wind managed 3.5 gigawatt hours on Saturday, against 147.9 on Tuesday 27 October [1]. When the wind drops, dearer plants run to fill the gap, and they set the price. The shape of Monday. The cheapest hour is 12:00 to 13:00 CET at €210.00. The dearest is 07:00 to 08:00 CET at €328.35, as the working week switches on [1]. Desk arithmetic: the morning peak costs about 56% more than lunchtime. The calm point. Every one of these numbers was published before the hours they describe, free for anyone to read. If you have a dynamic tariff, the midday hours are where the dishwasher belongs today. Nothing here is investment advice.

brent-near-111-on-talks-in-doha-and-thre.title: Brent near $111 on talks in Doha, and three numbers for the range
brent-near-111-on-talks-in-doha-and-thre.dek: Oil fell at Monday's open as Iran and Qatar talked for a third day. The banks' scenarios show how wide the road still is.
brent-near-111-on-talks-in-doha-and-thre.text: Brent crude futures fell $2.27, or 2%, to $111 a barrel early on Monday, and US WTI dropped 2.32% to $102, the Economic Times reported [1]. The trigger was diplomacy: Iranian and Qatari officials held a third consecutive day of talks aimed at ending the war [1]. Brent rose 13.6% in October, Reuters noted, so Monday’s fall takes back only a small part of that [2]. OPEC+ agreed over the weekend to keep its production targets unchanged through December, NDTV Profit reported [3]. Three numbers for the range. Goldman Sachs estimates crude could rise to $120 if attacks on ships in the Middle East escalate, or fall towards $80 if exports return to normal, the Economic Times reported [1]. Saxo Bank expects a $70 to $90 range even after the conflict ends, against $60 to $70 before the war [1]. Neither is a promise; both are stated assumptions you can check later. The physical side. Saudi Arabia raised its crude exports in October from September despite Houthi attacks on its energy infrastructure, according to two of three ship-tracking companies [1]. Last Thursday an unidentified projectile hit a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations [1]. Talks move prices in a morning. Cargoes move them for a season. Nothing here is investment advice.

102-5-for-gas-and-storage-at-74-62-on-th.title: €102.5 for gas, and storage at 74.62% on the first of November
102-5-for-gas-and-storage-at-74-62-on-th.dek: Europe's gas price eased with the oil price on Monday. The number that matters for winter is the one in the tanks.
102-5-for-gas-and-storage-at-74-62-on-th.text: European natural gas fell to €102.5 per megawatt hour on Monday as diplomatic efforts in the Middle East eased fears of further escalation, Trading Economics reported [1]. Iran and Qatar held talks in Doha for a third consecutive day [1]. The price is the noisy part. The quieter number is Europe’s gas storage: 74.62% full as of 1 November, Trading Economics said, a historically low level going into winter [1]. LNG supplies from the Persian Gulf remain severely disrupted while shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is threatened, and withdrawals have already begun in several countries as temperatures fall [1]. A tank does not react to a headline. It fills or empties one cargo and one cold night at a time, and that is what you can check each morning. Nothing here is investment advice.

three-central-banks-four-days-and-the-mi.title: Three central banks, four days, and the minutes matter more than the move
three-central-banks-four-days-and-the-mi.dek: Markets expect Canberra, London and Stockholm to raise rates this week. The useful part will be what each committee writes next to its number.
three-central-banks-four-days-and-the-mi.text: This is a committee week. Markets are betting on rate rises from the Reserve Bank of Australia, the Bank of England and Sweden’s Riksbank, and on Norway’s Norges Bank holding, Reuters reported [3]. None of that is a decision yet. It is a price, and prices can be wrong. Tuesday, Sydney. Of 40 economists and experts polled by Finder, 30 expect the RBA to lift its cash rate on Tuesday from 4.60% to 4.85% [2]. That would be the fifth rise this year. Headline inflation was 4.3% in September and the trimmed mean 3.6%, above the RBA’s 2–3% target band, as panellist Jeffrey Sheen noted while arguing for a hold [2]. Thursday, London. Economists polled by Reuters expect the Bank of England to raise Bank Rate to 4.0% from 3.75%, its first rise since August 2023, probably on a 7–2 vote [1]. UK consumer prices rose 3.5% in the year to September, against the Bank’s July forecast of 3.0% [1]. Markets price three to four more quarter-point rises in 2027, which Reuters says even the committee’s hawks may baulk at [1]. “Their hands are increasingly being forced,” said Rabobank’s Stefan Koopman [1]. The detail worth reading. Oxford Economics’ Alexander Harvey said individual members’ statements would offer important clues [1]. That is the dull machinery at work: minutes, votes and forecasts, published on a timetable, with names attached. A rise you can see coming is less painful than one you can’t, and a committee that says plainly how far it intends to go saves the market from guessing. In the US, futures still imply a 72% chance of a Fed rise in December, Reuters reported [3]. For you. If you hold a tracker mortgage or savings priced off one of these rates, Tuesday and Thursday are the dates to note. Nothing here is investment advice.

75-expect-it-55-want-it-the-gap-in-austr.title: 75% expect it, 55% want it: the gap in Australia's rate survey
75-expect-it-55-want-it-the-gap-in-austr.dek: Most of Finder's panel thinks the RBA will raise rates on Tuesday. Fewer think it should. The household arithmetic sits in between.
75-expect-it-55-want-it-the-gap-in-austr.text: Forecasting and judging are different jobs. Finder’s monthly panel of 40 economists and experts shows the difference. 75% (30 of 40) expect the Reserve Bank of Australia to raise its cash rate on Tuesday, to 4.85% [1]. Only 55% (22 of 40) say it should [1]. What it costs. Finder estimates that a quarter-point rise adds A$55 a month, or A$658 a year, to repayments on a A$500,000 mortgage [1]. Since January the cash rate would have risen 1.25 percentage points, which Finder puts at roughly A$258 a month on the same loan [1]. In Finder’s own consumer tracker, 37% of mortgage holders said they struggled to pay their home loan in October [1]. The case for waiting. Bendigo Bank’s David Robertson tipped a hold. He said that “having already increased rates 4 times this year the RBA can pause” [1]. Shane Oliver of AMP expects a rise, saying the RBA has “little choice” after September’s inflation data [1]. The quieter finding. Just over a third of those who answered (12 of 34) now think a recession in the next six months is likely, up from 30% in September [1]. A survey is not a decision, and the board meets with more data than any panel. But a published poll with named people and stated reasons is a useful thing: you can check them afterwards. Nothing here is investment advice.

gold-fell-6-8-in-october-the-yuan-sits-n.title: Gold fell 6.8% in October; the yuan sits near a four-year high
gold-fell-6-8-in-october-the-yuan-sits-n.dek: Monday's currency desks were quiet. The movement was in metal, and in China's exporters converting their dollars.
gold-fell-6-8-in-october-the-yuan-sits-n.text: The euro was flat at $1.1156 early on Monday and the dollar was barely changed at 157.62 yen, Reuters reported [1]. The action was elsewhere. Gold bounced 0.6% to $3,898 an ounce after falling 6.8% in October, Reuters reported. It had hit a one-year low amid talk that stressed investors were selling to meet margin calls [1]. A safe haven gets sold when people need cash quickly, because it is the easiest thing to sell. The Chinese yuan stayed near a more than four-year high against the dollar, Investing.com reported, helped by exporters converting foreign-currency earnings into yuan [2]. That is an exchange rate moved by invoices being paid, not by speeches. Nothing here is investment advice.

ordinary-ledger-174-per-100-litres-13-be.title: Ordinary Ledger: €174 per 100 litres, €13 between Hamburg and Hesse
ordinary-ledger-174-per-100-litres-13-be.dek: Heating oil starts November flat on the week, a third dearer than in summer and nearly double last year. The cheapest variable is still the date you order.
ordinary-ledger-174-per-100-litres-13-be.text: If your house heats with oil, the ledger this morning has one line that matters, and it is quieter than the headlines. The price. FastEnergy’s national average for standard heating oil, for a 3,000-litre order including delivery and VAT, was €174.23 per 100 litres at 05:10 this morning [1]. That is down 83 cents on yesterday and 78 cents on a week ago [1]. Further back the picture is less kind: €165.54 a month ago, €133.17 three months ago and €95.90 a year ago, a rise of 81.68% over the year [1]. The map. Where you live matters almost as much as when. FastEnergy’s state table put Hamburg lowest this morning at €165.92 and Hesse highest at €178.97 [1]. Berlin, Bremen and Brandenburg each fell by around €2.40 to €2.50 overnight; Saarland and Thuringia did not move [1]. The company puts the regional gaps down to supply routes, competition between dealers and local demand [1]. Desk arithmetic: the €13.05 per 100 litres between Hamburg and Hesse is about €390 on a 3,000-litre order. What’s in the litre. Most of the price is not the dealer’s. In FastEnergy’s breakdown, purchase costs are about two-thirds, VAT about 16%, the CO₂ charge about 8.6% and the fixed oil tax 6.14 cents a litre; the dealer’s own margin and costs are 2.48% [1]. That is why a move in crude never passes through to your bill one for one. What you can do. The advice is unglamorous: watch the market, avoid emergency orders, order a larger amount if you can, and consider a joint order with neighbours [1]. Ordering together spreads the delivery cost; a gauge checked now avoids the phone call in January. Nothing here is investment advice.

from-20-november-a-no-from-a-machine-can.title: From 20 November, a 'no' from a machine can be put to a human
from-20-november-a-no-from-a-machine-can.dek: The new EU credit rules are known for the pay-later check. Two quieter clauses matter as much: human review of automated refusals, and a time limit on withdrawal.
from-20-november-a-no-from-a-machine-can.text: In 18 days Germany starts applying the EU’s revised consumer credit directive, known as CCD II, to every credit contract signed from 20 November [1]. The headline part is familiar: small loans up to €200, some interest-free financing and many “buy now, pay later” offers now come under credit law, and lenders must check more carefully whether you can repay [1]. The clause worth remembering. Credit checks are increasingly automated. If a decision rests on automated processing of your personal data, you can, under the legal conditions, ask for an explanation and a review by a human [1]. The European Consumer Centre Germany, the EVZ, names it as a tip in its own right: if an application is refused automatically, ask for the reasons and whether a human review is due [1]. Lenders may also no longer use data on health, ethnic origin, political or religious views, or from your social media [1]. The clause worth watching. The so-called “eternal” right of withdrawal largely ends. Where required contract information is missing, withdrawal now lapses at the latest 12 months and 14 days after signing, unless you were never told of the right at all [1]. Overdrafts also gain a withdrawal right [1]. For you. Before 20 November nothing changes for contracts already signed [1]. After it, add up all open instalments, not just the monthly one, as the EVZ advises, and keep the paperwork [1]. A rule only protects people who know it exists. Nothing here is investment advice.

47-15-a-month-in-hamm-or-12-31-if-you-sw.title: €47.15 a month in Hamm, or €12.31 if you switch
47-15-a-month-in-hamm-or-12-31-if-you-sw.dek: One municipal utility's price letter shows the cost of staying on the default tariff.
47-15-a-month-in-hamm-or-12-31-if-you-sw.text: After three years of price cuts, Stadtwerke Hamm is raising its prices from 1 January 2027, blaming higher procurement costs, especially for gas [1]. In the basic gas tariff, the unit price rises by 2.68 cents per kWh and the standing charge by €29.75 a year, gross [1]. For a household using 20,000 kWh, that is €47.15 more a month, or 23.54% [1]. The same household moving to one of the utility’s special gas products would pay only €12.31 a month more than before [1]. Electricity in the basic tariff rises by 3.87 cents per kWh plus €23.80 a year; at 3,000 kWh that is €11.66 a month, or 12.51% [1]. Desk arithmetic: the gap between staying and switching on gas is €34.84 a month, about €418 a year. The cheapest tariff is often the one next door, at the same company.

the-annex-a-judge-reads-mobile-source-an.title: The Annex: a judge reads 'mobile source' and finds a power plant
the-annex-a-judge-reads-mobile-source-an.dek: xAI argued its gas turbines were exempt and that the people suing it had no right to. A federal court in Mississippi said no to both, and the case moves on to the facts.
the-annex-a-judge-reads-mobile-source-an.text: The document. Late on Friday, the US District Court for the Northern District of Mississippi released an opinion denying xAI’s motion to dismiss a Clean Air Act lawsuit brought by the NAACP [1][2]. The suit, filed in April by the Southern Environmental Law Center and Earthjustice, concerns gas-fired turbines in Southaven, Mississippi, that power the company’s Colossus data centres across the state line in Greater Memphis [1]. It alleges that between August and December 2025 xAI and a subsidiary installed and ran 27 turbines “without an air permit” [1]. xAI is now owned by SpaceX, which CNBC says has rebranded it SpaceXAI [1]. The three arguments. xAI’s lawyers, in a motion filed in June, said the turbines were “mobile” and so exempt from permitting; that the NAACP had no right to sue under the Act; and that citizen suits of this kind are unconstitutional [1]. The court’s answer fits in one sentence, which CNBC quotes: “Because the plaintiffs have statutory standing under the Clean Air Act, because the combustion turbines are not ‘mobile sources’ under Mississippi’s SIP, and because the citizen suit provision does not violate Article II of the Constitution or the private nondelegation doctrine, the plaintiffs’ claims will proceed.” [1] The line that matters for every data centre. The plant “was not (and is not) exempted from permitting requirements,” the court held, according to Earthjustice, because it is not a mobile source under the federal regulations [2]. Read plainly: a generator on a trailer is still a power station if it behaves like one. For an industry racing to put electricity next to its chips faster than the grid can deliver it, that sentence moves the permit back to the front of the queue. What it does not say. The opinion lets the claims proceed [1]; it is not a finding that xAI broke the law. The court has not yet decided the NAACP’s request for a preliminary injunction [2]. About two weeks earlier, the same court rejected a Department of Justice request to end the case [1]. The emissions figures in circulation, more than 5,000 tons a year of nitrogen oxides among them, are the plaintiffs’ side’s estimates of what the turbines can emit [2]. The constructive reading. The dull machinery worked as designed: a permit rule, a citizen-suit clause written decades ago, and a judge who read both. Compute will need a great deal of power. The paperwork that comes with power plants is how the neighbours get a say.

one-allowance-for-everything-counted-in-.title: One allowance for everything, counted in tokens
one-allowance-for-everything-counted-in-.dek: From December, ChatGPT's Plus, Pro and Business plans share a single budget across chat and Codex. The all-you-can-prompt era ends with a support page.
one-allowance-for-everything-counted-in-.text: The most consequential product change of the weekend arrived as a help-centre article. “Starting in December,” OpenAI writes, the usage allowance on Plus, Pro and Business plans “will be shared across ChatGPT and Codex”, as the agent features of its Work mode move into the main ChatGPT experience [1]. Usage will be measured in tokens, the units a model reads and writes, and how fast you spend them depends on the model and the task: more advanced models and complex tasks use more [1]. Chat with the Instant models will not count against the allowance [1]. Your remaining balance and reset times will sit under Settings → Usage; when it runs out, you can wait, upgrade, or buy credits [1]. OpenAI says it expects most users “won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do now” [1]. The Decoder reads it as the end of flat-rate prompting for heavy users, noting that OpenAI recently doubled limits on its pricier plans and that users currently choose between two operating modes and 11 model settings [2]. Anthropic has already combined chat and “Cowork” in Claude, it adds [2]. The constructive reading is the boring one. A meter is not a betrayal; it is an invoice you can read. Once the December date is set, check Settings → Usage after a normal week before deciding whether you need a bigger plan.

apple-reports-tonight-at-22-30-with-a-ne.title: Apple reports tonight at 22:30, with a new chief executive on the call
apple-reports-tonight-at-22-30-with-a-ne.dek: The guidance was 9 to 11% growth. The release will say whether memory prices ate any of it.
apple-reports-tonight-at-22-30-with-a-ne.text: Apple publishes its fiscal fourth-quarter results today at 1:30pm Pacific time, which is 22:30 in Berlin now that both sides have left summer time; the call with new chief executive John Ternus and finance chief Kevan Parekh follows at 23:00 [1]. The quarter ran from 28 June to 26 September and includes only launch-week sales of the iPhone 18 Pro [1]. On the previous quarter’s call, Parekh guided to total revenue growth of 9 to 11%, with iPhone growth in the mid-teens despite currency headwinds and supply constraints [1]. On last year’s $102.5 billion, MacRumors puts that at $111.7 billion to $113.7 billion [1]. Watch for what management says about memory pricing and supply [1]. The figure that matters is the company’s own; ours would be a guess. Nothing here is investment advice.

855-shortage-notices-and-a-list-that-let.title: 855 shortage notices, and a list that lets the pharmacist decide
855-shortage-notices-and-a-list-that-let.dek: Germany's drug shortage register starts November with hundreds of open entries, many of them children's antibiotics. The fix that works is procedural, not heroic.
855-shortage-notices-and-a-list-that-let.text: Winter coughs are coming, and the register of medicines that are hard to get is not short. A summary of the federal drug agency’s shortage database, compiled by the pharmacy news site Apotheke Aktuell from BfArM’s export with data as of 30 October, counts 855 active notices [1]. Of those, 259 are classed as relevant to supply, 195 as critical to supply, and 246 as relevant to hospitals [1]. A notice is per product and strength, so one active ingredient can appear many times. The children’s shelf. Several of the critical entries are what a paediatrician reaches for in November. Amoxicillin AL dry suspension has been listed since May 2024, citing higher demand, with an expected end of 1 December 2026 [1]. Cefaclor and cefuroxime suspensions from several makers are marked critical; so is a penicillin V granulate from 1 A Pharma, until 30 November [1]. A salbutamol inhaler, Bronchospray Autohaler, is critical until February 2027 [1]. For adults, the list carries the everyday: pantoprazole, atorvastatin and escitalopram from some makers [1]. The machinery. None of that means the pharmacy will send you home empty-handed. BfArM keeps a separate urgency list of essential children’s medicines that may be in tight supply, last updated with data as of 15 October [2]. For a drug on that list, a pharmacy that cannot supply the prescribed product may swap it for one with the same active ingredient made up in the pharmacy, or for a ready-made product in a different form, without first calling the doctor [2]. The list is refreshed roughly every 14 days [2]. BfArM’s own news page shows the rest of the routine: an updated overview of imported injectable aspirin on 27 October, and on 23 October the current children’s medicine list under the shortage law, the ALBVVG [3]. For you. If a child’s antibiotic is not on the shelf, ask the pharmacist about a substitute in another form before you go back to the surgery; the rules now allow it for listed medicines [2]. And if you take a regular tablet, order the next pack a week earlier than usual this winter. It costs nothing, and it gives the supply chain the one thing it lacks: time.

cutting-the-dose-does-not-spare-the-baby.title: Cutting the dose does not spare the baby, a cord-tissue study finds
cutting-the-dose-does-not-spare-the-baby.dek: Pregnant women treated for opioid use disorder are sometimes urged to take less. Measurements from 92 pregnancies found no link between dose and the newborn's withdrawal.
cutting-the-dose-does-not-spare-the-baby.text: Methadone and buprenorphine are the two medicines commonly used to treat opioid use disorder in pregnancy [1]. A worry that higher doses bring worse withdrawal in the newborn leads some patients and clinicians to consider lowering the dose or stopping [1]. A research letter in JAMA Network Open, published on 29 October by researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, tested that worry directly [1]. The method. The team analysed 92 pregnancies in which the mother had taken methadone or buprenorphine for at least 30 days before delivery, and measured the drugs and their breakdown products in umbilical cord tissue, a marker of what the baby was exposed to over the final trimester [1]. Severe withdrawal occurred in about 44% of the newborns, more often after methadone than buprenorphine [1]. But neither the mother’s dose nor the cord concentration was significantly linked to how severe it was [1]. “Cutting the dose doesn’t give the baby an easier withdrawal. It only puts the mother at risk,” said Courtney Townsel, the lead author [1]. The limits. The sample is small and not very diverse, the authors say, and the result does not mean newborns need less monitoring or care [1]. What it does is remove a reason to under-treat the mother. For you. If you or someone close to you is in this position, the finding supports a simple sequence: set the dose for the mother’s recovery, and let the hospital look after the baby’s withdrawal if it comes. Treatment kept is protection kept.

r6-39-off-the-hpv-vial-south-africas-vac.title: R6.39 off the HPV vial: South Africa's vaccine invoice gets lighter
r6-39-off-the-hpv-vial-south-africas-vac.dek: Four state vaccine contract prices fell on Sunday after currency moves. Small numbers, and the dull machinery of public health.
r6-39-off-the-hpv-vial-south-africas-vac.text: From Sunday, South Africa’s immunisation programme pays a little less for four vaccines [1]. The Department of Health attributes the cuts, signed on 14 October, to favourable exchange-rate changes [1]. Under the contract, the rotavirus vaccine falls from R124.46 to R122.32, the HPV vaccine from R372.77 to R366.38, a combined tetanus, diphtheria and pertussis booster from R152.28 to R150.01, and BCG from R150.85 to R148.24 [1]. The reductions are about 1.5% to 1.7% [1]. These are prices per contract unit, including VAT and delivery, not charges to patients, and the notices give no quantities, so no total saving can be worked out [1]. The useful lesson is elsewhere: when a contract is written to pass currency gains back to the buyer, the buyer notices. Most vaccine news is about fear. This one is about an invoice.

433-drones-in-a-night-and-the-repair-cre.title: 433 drones in a night, and the repair crews' ledger
433-drones-in-a-night-and-the-repair-cre.dek: Russia's winter campaign against Ukraine's grid is counted in substations. The answer is counted in interceptors and in people who climb poles.
433-drones-in-a-night-and-the-repair-cre.text: Overnight into Sunday, Russia launched 433 drones at Ukraine, including jet-powered Shaheds; Ukraine’s air force said it downed 371 [1]. Drones struck 16 locations and debris fell in 14 more [1]. Regional authorities reported one person killed, in Sloviansk, and at least 47 injured across the country, among them three children in Dnipropetrovsk region and a 16-year-old girl in Kharkiv region [1]. Desk arithmetic: 62 drones got through the air defences, about one in seven. The target was again the grid. President Volodymyr Zelensky named substations, transformers and power lines in four regions, Dnipro, Vinnytsia, Zhytomyr and Khmelnytskyi, and said “hundreds of thousands of families remain without electricity” [2]. Three workers from the energy company DTEK were injured, and DTEK introduced emergency outages in Kyiv [1]. In Sumy region, the administration said air-raid sirens sounded for 23 hours 57 minutes of the day [1]. Zelensky also gave the week’s ledger: 1,940 strike drones, more than 1,580 glide bombs and 44 missiles, 36 of them ballistic [2]. “The Russians are trying to take maximum advantage of the shortage of ballistic interceptors,” he said, asking allies to implement air-defence decisions “now” [1][2]. That is a supply-chain sentence as much as a military one: the war’s winter will be decided partly in factories and delivery schedules far from Ukraine. What went right is quieter. Crews are “working to restore damaged equipment, when it is safe to do so”, DTEK said [1]; Zelensky said repair crews were “working everywhere” [2]. Each restored line is a small, unreported victory over a much louder weapon. For you, the useful number is not the drones launched but the hours without power, and who is paid to shorten them.

kstovo-by-night-what-kyiv-calls-long-ran.title: Kstovo by night: what Kyiv calls "long-range sanctions"
kstovo-by-night-what-kyiv-calls-long-ran.dek: Ukraine's answer to the grid war is aimed at refineries and plants deep inside Russia. The claims are large; the verified facts are smaller, and worth keeping apart.
kstovo-by-night-what-kyiv-calls-long-ran.text: On Sunday the governor of Russia’s Nizhny Novgorod region, Gleb Nikitin, said an “industrial enterprise” in the Kstovo district had been hit by a “massive drone attack” overnight, causing “significant damage” [1]. He said more than 100 drones were destroyed and no casualties had been reported so far [1]. Ukrainian media reports said the strike hit the LukOil refinery in Kstovo and a combined heat and power plant; RFE/RL said it could not independently verify that [1]. Video shared on Sunday appears to show the refinery in flames [1]. Less than 24 hours earlier, Ukraine’s military said it had targeted the Kombinat Kamensky chemical and defence enterprise in Russia’s Rostov region with drones and Neptune missiles, and Zelensky said that attack caused “tens of millions of dollars” of damage [1]. Kyiv calls these strikes “long-range sanctions” [1]. The phrase is worth taking literally. A sanction works through inventories: a refinery that cannot run is fuel that is not shipped, taxed or burned at the front, and the effect shows up weeks later in export volumes and pump prices, not in the night’s video. So keep two columns. In the first, what officials on each side say, attributed. In the second, what independent records later confirm: refinery run rates, export loadings, repair notices. The second column is slower and duller. It is also the one that tells you whether the “sanction” bit.

latvia-takes-the-chair-at-the-security-c.title: Latvia takes the chair at the Security Council
latvia-takes-the-chair-at-the-security-c.dek: A one-month presidency is mostly procedure. Procedure, its ambassador notes, can be highly political.
latvia-takes-the-chair-at-the-security-c.text: Since Sunday, 1 November, Latvia has presided over the UN Security Council, for the first time in its history [1]. The presidency rotates monthly in English alphabetical order; Greece had October, Liberia takes December [1]. Its ambassador, Sanita Pavļuta-Deslandes, says about 90% of the Council’s agenda is mandated and regular meetings, leaving room for “one or two signature events” [1]. Latvia’s are Ukraine and technology: the Council’s new informal expert group on technology, peace and security, set up on 23 October at Latvia’s and Greece’s initiative, holds its first meeting this month [1]. On 3 November Latvia also presides over the election of judges to the International Court of Justice, and a vote on extending the Yemen sanctions regime is expected [1]. The Council has adopted 19 resolutions this year, the ministry says [1]. Small states do not win arguments at the UN by volume. They win them by chairing the meeting well.

from-60-to-261-in-two-days-delhis-smog-s.title: From 60 to 261 in two days: Delhi's smog season opens on schedule
from-60-to-261-in-two-days-delhis-smog-s.dek: Friday's rain gave the capital clean air; by Sunday night the index was at 290. The rules arrived on the same morning as the smoke, which is the point of having rules.
from-60-to-261-in-two-days-delhis-smog-s.text: On Friday, after heavy rain and strong winds, Delhi recorded an air quality index of 60, “satisfactory” [1]. On Saturday it was 117. On Sunday the official 24-hour average reached 261, “poor”, and it kept climbing through the evening: 272 at 6pm, 287 at 10pm, 290 at 11pm local time [1]. It is the worst reading since 17 April, the Times of India notes, and the highest in 198 days [2]. Of the city’s 57 reporting stations, 22 were in the “very poor” band; Jahangirpuri was worst at 378, not far below the “severe” line at 401 [2]. The weather did not cause the smoke. It stopped carrying it away. Delhi’s minimum on Sunday was 18 degrees, 1.9 below the seasonal average, and a Hindustan Times reading of the Safdarjung weather balloon found the day’s pollution mixed only 1,100 metres up, in winds averaging 10 km/h; on a typical early-November afternoon it is about 1,300 metres and 13 km/h [1]. A lower lid and a slower breeze: the same emissions, less room. The model view tells the same story in fine particles. Open-Meteo’s CAMS series for a central Delhi grid point shows PM2.5 near 80 µg/m³ early last week, a dip to 28.8 on Friday after the rain, and a return to 81.0 by Sunday [3]. Desk arithmetic: the rain bought roughly two days. Where it comes from matters more than the number. The government’s decision-support system put stubble burning at 18.57% of Delhi’s pollution on Sunday, up from 5.33% on Saturday; transport inside the city was 16.4% [1][2]. One analyst told the HT that two-thirds of the fine particles come from outside the city [1]. A city cannot legislate its neighbours’ fields, which is why the answer is a calendar, not a speech. That calendar started on Sunday. Non-Delhi vehicles below BS-VI standards are barred, dust-generating outdoor construction is banned until 31 January, parking charges are doubled until 28 February, and offices are capped at 50% attendance [2]. It brought queues at the borders and grumbling online [2]. Rules that inconvenience people on the first day are usually the ones that are actually enforced.

fog-below-150-metres-frost-to-minus-thre.title: Fog below 150 metres, frost to minus three, and a week of ageing polar air
fog-below-150-metres-frost-to-minus-thre.dek: Germany's November opens quiet, grey and cold at night. The DWD's week reads like a list of reasons to leave five minutes early.
fog-below-150-metres-frost-to-minus-thre.text: High pressure and ageing polar air set Germany’s weather this week, the Deutscher Wetterdienst wrote at 05:00 this morning, with a weak front from the North Sea bringing a little rain to the northwest [1]. Nothing dramatic is forecast, and quiet weeks are when the small preparations get done. This morning, the centre and south have patchy dense fog, with visibility below 150 metres, and light frost down to -3 degrees across much of the southern half [1]. Today’s highs run from 4 to 12 degrees, with little wind except on the North Sea, where gusts around 55 km/h from the north to north-east reach the East Frisian Islands into Tuesday night [1]. On the High Black Forest summits, easterly gusts of 60 to 75 km/h are possible [1]. Tuesday stays cloudy, with drizzle from the west across the northwest to the north-east and highs of about 4 degrees on high ground in the south and 11 on the North Sea [1]. Wednesday is dry and murky at the Alpine edge, at 5 degrees, and up to 10 elsewhere [1]. Thursday brings stubborn fog first, then sunny spells; on the night into Friday, light frost of 0 to -4 degrees is widespread away from the coast and the far north [1]. So: a scraper in the car, dipped headlights in the fog, and a radiator that is bled before the cold arrives rather than after. The forecast is the DWD’s; the windscreen is yours.

one-week-to-antalya-and-a-timetable-alre.title: One week to Antalya, and a timetable already in print
one-week-to-antalya-and-a-timetable-alre.dek: COP31 opens on 9 November. The host has published a theme for each day, which is a more useful document than any opening speech.
one-week-to-antalya-and-a-timetable-alre.text: The UN climate conference, COP31, runs in Antalya from 9 to 20 November, the United Nations says [1]. The leaders’ summit is on 11 and 12 November [2]. The detailed session programme is still to come, but the Turkish presidency has printed a theme for each day [2]. Monday 9 November is food, agriculture and health; Tuesday energy and transport; Wednesday zero waste and methane; Thursday resilient cities and disaster risk management; Friday 13 November finance, trade and carbon markets [2]. The second week moves through science and industry, then oceans and land use, and the last themed day, 19 November, is “İmece: Enhancing Implementation” – capacity building, investment-ready projects and access to finance [2]. Read the last line twice. A conference that ends on implementation is admitting where the gap is. Judge it in a fortnight by projects with a budget, not by the leaders’ paragraphs.

de-power-day-ahead-02nov.title: No cheap weekend this time: €259.31 for Monday
de-power-day-ahead-02nov.subtitle: Germany/Luxembourg day-ahead electricity price, daily average by delivery day, € per MWh
de-power-day-ahead-02nov.source: Bundesnetzagentur | SMARD.de, day-ahead price DE-LU (filter 4169), delivery days 1 Sep to 2 Nov 2026, retrieved 2 Nov 2026 · CC BY 4.0
de-power-day-ahead-02nov.alt: Line chart of the daily average German-Luxembourg day-ahead electricity price from 1 September to 2 November 2026, in euros per megawatt hour. It reaches a September high of €256.55 on 14 September, falls to €30.12 on Saturday 24 October and €13.12 on Sunday 25 October during the storm, then climbs to €314.85 on Thursday 29 October, the highest daily average of 2026 so far, and €268.62 on Friday 30 October. This weekend stayed high: €251.42 on Saturday 31 October and €255.91 on Sunday 1 November. The latest value is €259.31 for delivery on Monday 2 November.

delhi-pm25-02nov.title: The rain washed it out, the smoke came back in two days
delhi-pm25-02nov.subtitle: Fine particles (PM2.5), daily mean, µg/m³ · central Delhi grid point (modelled), 26 Oct – 1 Nov 2026, India time
delhi-pm25-02nov.source: Open-Meteo Air Quality API (open-meteo.com), hourly PM2.5 from the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS) model at 28.6°N 77.2°E, desk daily means of 24 hourly values (Asia/Kolkata days); retrieved 2 Nov 2026 · Open-Meteo data CC BY 4.0, contains Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service information. Modelled grid values, not CPCB station readings.

us-midterm-stress-02nov.title: Stressed by the vote, still planning to cast it

us-midterm-stress-02nov.alt: Bar chart from a LifeStance survey of 1,000 US adults in October 2026: 70% feel at least some stress about the 3 November midterms; 55% of Gen Z, 51% of full-time employees, 48% of millennials and 43% of all adults report moderate or significant stress; 32% have a plan to protect their mental health on election night; 26% have used an AI chatbot to talk through election stress.

ust-october-curve-02nov.title: October's rally reached every maturity except the bills
ust-october-curve-02nov.subtitle: Fall in US Treasury par yields over October, Wed 30 Sep to Fri 30 Oct 2026, basis points (one basis point = 0.01 percentage point)
ust-october-curve-02nov.source: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates, 30 Sep and 30 Oct 2026 (home.treasury.gov), retrieved 2 Nov 2026 · U.S. government data, public domain · Bars are desk arithmetic: the difference between the two closing yields.
ust-october-curve-02nov.alt: Bar chart of how far US Treasury par yields fell over October 2026, from Wednesday 30 September to Friday 30 October, in basis points. The 3-month yield fell 4, from 4.20% to 4.16%. The 2-year fell 32, from 4.88% to 4.56%. The 5-year fell 38, from 5.09% to 4.71%, the largest move. The 10-year fell 35, from 5.29% to 4.94%. The 30-year fell 33, from 5.64% to 5.31%. The latest values are the 30 October closes.

china-pmi-falls-02nov.title: Prices and production fell furthest; export orders more than the headline
china-pmi-falls-02nov.subtitle: Fall in China's official manufacturing PMI and selected sub-indices, September to October 2026, index points (50 separates expansion from contraction)
china-pmi-falls-02nov.source: National Bureau of Statistics of China, official manufacturing PMI for October 2026, published 31 Oct 2026, as reported by Xinhua and The Asia Business Daily · the export-orders bar is desk arithmetic from the two reported readings · retrieved 2 Nov 2026
china-pmi-falls-02nov.alt: Bar chart of how far China's official manufacturing PMI and selected sub-indices fell from September to October 2026, in index points. The headline PMI fell 0.8, from 50.1 to 49.3. Production fell 1.9 to 49.8. New orders fell 1.1 to 49.4. New export orders fell 1.3, from 50.0 to 48.7 (desk arithmetic). The large-firm PMI fell 0.4 to 50.2. Factory-gate prices fell 2.3 to 51.7. Purchase prices fell 4.0 to 56.8, the largest fall. All figures are for October 2026, the latest month.
